title: Exploring Tulare County's most haunted homes, hotels and graves
excerpt: From apparitions at the Zalud House to phantom laughter at The Depot, Tulare County is rich with ghost stories. For Halloween, explore the legends that endure.
content:
Oct. 16, 2026, 2:00 a.m. PT

From a bullet-pierced chair in the Zalud House to reports of phantom laughter echoing through The Depot's dining room, Tulare County is full of places where haunted history and ghost stories collide.

Whether they're viewed as local folklore or evidence of something paranormal, stories of unexplained encounters have been passed down for generations. Investigators, historians and longtime residents recount tales of apparitions, cold spots and ghostly voices at landmarks across the county.

For Halloween, the Visalia Times-Delta explores some of Tulare County's best-known haunted locations and the stories that keep their legends alive.

The Zalud House: Ghosts in the mirror?

In October 2025, professional ghost hunter and author Marie Mason conducted paranormal investigation tours at the Zalud House Museum in Porterville, which was built in 1891 by John Zalud and his wife, Mary.

“Annie, one of the daughters, married a guy named William,” she said. “He was accused of having an affair with a woman. When William and his friends were in the old Pioneer Hotel, a gentleman's club, they were sitting in the lobby and this lady that accused him of having an affair came in, and they were laughing at her.” 

The woman was planning to take her life, according to the story.

“When she came into the hotel, she saw William sitting there laughing at her,” Mason said. “She turned the gun on him and shot four times.” 

The chair, which still has a bullet hole in it, was later moved to the Zalud House where it was put on display upstairs in William’s room.

William’s room also has a mirror, which during one of the investigations had clear image of a man, according to Mason. 

“I told every guest, take a picture,” she said. “Once you put the camera up to this mirror, a full apparition face is in this mirror, a high forehead, a man's haircut. And then on the wall in that same room is a portrait of William, and that's him.”

The investigation went to Pearl’s room, where the last surviving daughter slept.

“In the room on a mannequin is Pearl's really pretty lacy dress,” Mason said. “I have equipment that detects energy in a form of stick figures. When we were upstairs in Pearl's room, her dress was energetic and there was a stick figure inside her dress, like Pearl was trapped in her dress."

To Mason, the investigation provided “confirmation that those people are still here, confirmation that that the people that lived in the house still haunt the house.”

The Depot's unexplained encounters

When Visalia Times-Delta interviewed Armando Apodaca in November 2024, he confirmed rumors that The Depot in downtown Visalia is indeed haunted. He worked at the popular restaurant for 38 years.

“I, myself, used to hear every once in a while the laughter of a woman in the main dining room," he said. "At first, you'd hear the clinking of glasses like a party or something, and then she would laugh."

In the "Baggage Room," which served at the banquet room, there was what Apodaca called "The Malevolent One."

“You knew when he was there because – and I'm not a believer in ghosts – it would turn really, really cold and then you could feel a presence there, and not a good presence," Apodaca said. “The lights wouldn't work, or they would flicker and flicker, and they couldn't find that there was anything wrong with the lights."

The other apparition was in the bathroom, according to Apodaca.

“There were a couple of times when women told me, ‘I couldn't get out! I couldn't get out! And there was a smelly man in here,'" he said. “Several women told me that. They could smell a smelly man and he wouldn't let them out."

Apodaca said that he never saw (or smelled) that ghost.

Downtown Visalia's unseen residents

The Depot, which is on Oak Avenue, is in the most active paranormal area of Visalia, according to Anna Campbell, psychic, medium, and paranormal investigator. The area she described includes the former sites of Fort Visalia, the first county courthouse, a jail and a bordello.

“That is where we used to train people who wanted to investigate because there was such high intelligent activity,” said Campbell, who used to lead the Tulare County Paranormal Society. “We wanted to make sure those coming on weren't going to freak out and be scared, and we weeded out people down there. I would say probably eight out of 10 didn't make it.” 

In that area, she said she has encountered the spirits of those stationed at Fort Visalia, as well as “at least three of the ladies of the night from the bordello. 

“There is an extremely strong physical male presence down there,” she added. “I'm talking touching, hitting, throwing things, scratching. This is a man who was not nice here. It's not demonic or anything like that. It's just a man who does not like to be bothered, does not like you in his area."

He's between The Depot and Jack & Charlie's, she said.

The site of Visalia’s first schoolhouse also has spirits, Campbell said.

“Where the old schoolhouse was, out front in those trees there are some spirits that will be up there,” she said. “They'll throw down some things. They’re children from the old schoolhouse. It's like, ‘I'm pranking you.’”

An older woman lived by herself by the old schoolhouse, according to Campbell.

“She was very old and she was telling us about how she was tending her garden, and that she was getting irritated at the kids going to the school because they were trampling her garden,” she added, explaining that they communicated through Campbell’s EVP recording device.

The Lady in White of Springville Inn

The Springville Inn, which has 13 rooms, is rumored to have ghosts. Several ghost-hunting television shows have filmed segments there.

“They heard a lot of mumbling and talking, especially in one of the rooms, room nine,” said Joanna Rayani, co-owner of the hotel, which sees an increase in visitors because of the ghosts, especially in October. “In our suite, which is room 13, they were hearing footsteps."

The upstairs gets a lot of activity, Rayani said. On the first floor, there's always a lady dressed in a white dress. 

“It's usually around this time of the year that the workers start to see her,” she continued. “She'll walk by the cash register, and they're confused as to what's going on, because sometimes there's no customers in there."

The upstairs has been turned into a dough room, where pizza dough is made.

"My sister was up there, and she was walking down the hall," Rayani said. "All of a sudden, she got a white handprint on her. It was a flour handprint."

Rayani thinks that one reason for the unexplained activity may be the Tulare-Kings Joint Tubercu­lar Hospital that opened in Springville shortly after World War I to deal with the tuberculosis outbreak in the area.

Tulare County’s haunted cemeteries

Tulare County historian Dallas Pattee has studied and photographed cemeteries in Tulare County, and she shared two stories about the Visalia Public Cemetery.

“The main story is that there is a Union soldier ghost who haunts the cemetery, but we don't know his name,” Pattee said, before offering a theory. “We had two murder victims from Camp Babbitt, and I'm thinking it's one of them.

“People would be out (at) the cemetery tending to the graves of their friends and loved ones, and this image of a soldier dressed in blue would just appear before their eyes,” she said. “They were just kind of dumbstruck, and then it just vanished."

Pattee captured a white figure on film at Lone Oak Cemetery near Ivanhoe, where a party of settlers was massacred by members of a local tribe in 1851. A man with the last name of Woods led a party there from Mariposa the year before.

“Woods had come down there and tried to settle,” said historian and book publisher Chris Brewer. “The Indians told him, ‘No, don’t do that. We don’t want you here.' He did it anyway.”
